paragraphs.source_en: Shelters or rocks are commonly used for rain rituals. The Sandawe in Tanzania use big boulders in isolated places at a high altitude where they sacrifice domesticated cattle during rain rituals. The blood of the animal is spread on the boulder and then paintings of the sacrificed animal are created (Ten Raa 1969). A similar situation is documented for the Masai in Kenya using shelters for rain rituals. After they sacrifice a cow or bull a painting of it is made in the shelter (Le Quellec 2004). On the Tassili Plateau Tin Tekelt shelter has been used until recently for rain making rituals. There is a recent engraving representing a child's foot on which nomads pour milk and oil in the belief that it will attract rain.

paragraphs.source_en: This shelter also contains the remains of Round Head paintings and around 300 cupules, indicating the spiritual importance of the place since the prehistoric times until today.

paragraphs.source_en: Based on the ethnographic record it cannot be excluded that painted sites in the Central Sahara were also frequented for similar purposes. Numerous groups may have concentrated together in regular meetings at certain times of the year during which they would socialize, or they would unite for the occasion of large initiation camps. A limited number of persons selected under certain criteria, such as young boys or girls to be initiated, may have frequented painted shelters designated only for certain purposes or rituals. However, the function of the holy places could have changed in time, although remaining still important. This may be the case for some Round Head sites; firstly used by hunter-gatherers, these same sites were consequently frequented by pastoralists whose paintings were very different and so the purposes might have been very different as well.

paragraphs.source_en: Since the pastoralists sometimes painted in Round Head sites where they could not enter with their herds because of the difficult access or restricted space, it must be proposed that they were fully aware of the spiritual importance of such sites.
